newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: INTERVIEW - Intel sees strong Pentium II sale.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Intel sees strong Pentium II sale.

text.p: Intel Corp expects shipments of its latest Pentium II microprocessor to exceed that of Pentium Pro, despite a flaw in the chip, officials said on Tuesday.
They also said that Intel had received no complaints in the Asia Pacific region regarding the flaw in Pentium II chip dubbed "Flag Erratum".

"It's going to be very exciting. It's the follow-on generation from Pentium Pro and we expect it (shipment of Pentium II) to exceed Pentium Pro," Geoff Healey, Intel's regional sales and marketing manager, APAC server business told
Reuters ahead of the launch in Singapore.
He declined to reveal the expected or current volumes of shipments for both Pentium Pro and Pentium II.
Demand for Pentium II was seen strong globally with "balanced" shares between the Asia Pacific and Europe and slightly more from the United States, he said.

Martin Geh, Intel Singapore Technology Ltd's country manager, said Pentium II would be immediately available on "typically high volume PC systems that cost below US$2,500 each", boosting demand for both corporate and home use.
Computers based on Pentium Pro on the other hand took about nine months to drop to that price level, he said.
The Pentium II increases the production efficiency of the motherboard and hence lowers the cost of a computer, said Tony Jansz, Intel's regional sales manager, South Asia.
The company officials said Intel had posted software on its Web site for downloading to correct the flaw in Pentium II.

The "Flag Erratum" flaw occurs when some programs try to convert floating-point numbers, or decimals, into integers. In some cases, the chip makes rounding errors and it does not raise a warning flag that it made the error.
"In Singapore there has been no complaints so we haven't recorded any problems," said Geh.
"There has been a similar response on a regional level," Healey added.
Intel has said that no recall was needed for Pentium II.
Computer makers exhibiting Pentium II-based systems at the launch in Singapore agreed they did not see major problems with Pentium II.
"Errata is normal in microprocessors and we are working to reduce the number of errata," said Healey.
